Do the following using the steps provided in their respective sections.
        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis. 
            2.2 kubernetes yamls based on the analysis.
            2.3 github actions file to build application on pushing to main branch.
        3. add all changed file to git changes 
        4. commit / push to repo

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) to finish the whole workflow.  
I’ve also included the exact file contents that should end up in the repository.

> **NOTE** – The instructions assume you have `git`, `docker`, `kubectl` and `yq` (or any YAML editor) installed on the machine where you run them.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & create the artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo with the following content:

```Dockerfile
# Dockerfile for nodejs-welcome
# ---------------------------------
# Base image – lightweight Node runtime
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
```

> *Why this image?*  
> `node:18-alpine` is small, secure, and contains the latest LTS Node runtime.  
> If you prefer a different Node version, change the `FROM` line accordingly.

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s-nodejs-welcome.yaml` (or split into two files – `deployment.yaml` & `service.yaml`) with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> *What to replace?*  
> Replace `<YOUR_REGISTRY>` with the registry you’ll push to (e.g. `ghcr.io/zelarhq` or `docker.io/zelarhq`).  
> If you want a LoadBalancer or NodePort, change `type:` accordingly.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log in to Docker Hub (or your registry)
      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build \
            --tag ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} \
            --tag ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest \
            .

      # Push the image
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
          docker push ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Secrets required**  
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username (or registry user).  
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token with `write:packages` scope.  

> If you’re using GitHub Container Registry (GHCR), replace the login step with:

```yaml
- name: Log in to GHCR
  uses: docker/login-action@v3
  with:
    registry: ghcr.io
    username: ${{ github.actor }}
    password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
```

and adjust the image tags accordingly (`ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome`).

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s-nodejs-welcome.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

---

## 🎉 What’s next?

1. **Verify the CI** – After pushing, check the Actions tab in GitHub; the workflow should build and push the image.  
2. **Deploy to a cluster** – Apply the Kubernetes manifest:

   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s-nodejs-welcome.yaml
   ```

3. **Expose the service** – If you need external access, change the service type to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` and re‑apply.

That’s it! You now have a fully‑automated pipeline that builds a Docker image on every push to `main`, stores it in your registry, and you have ready‑to‑use Kubernetes manifests for deployment.
